note:
ISO 2026-W49 runs from November 30 through December 6. To find Mars, first identify Leo, trace the Sickle, and locate Regulus in that pattern. Mars lies about 1.7° away in ecliptic longitude at the Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot; use the finder to transfer from Regulus to the planet. To find Jupiter, first identify Leo, trace the Sickle, and locate Regulus in that pattern. Jupiter lies about 3.1° away in ecliptic longitude at the Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot; use the finder to transfer from Regulus to the planet.

**Naked eye:** 🌗 Last Quarter — 06:08:40 UTC. Moderate moonlight makes timing and local sky position important for faint targets. Use Achernar as the week’s fixed-sky framework.

**Planets:** Moon: Naked eye; magnitude -10.8; direct motion; 63.9% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Venus in ecliptic longitude Dec 05 05:41 UTC. Conjunction with Mars in ecliptic longitude Nov 30 17:24 UTC. Conjunction with Jupiter in ecliptic longitude Nov 30 08:34 UTC. Mercury: In solar glare; magnitude -0.7; direct motion; 83.1% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Venus: Naked eye; magnitude -4.9; direct motion; 26.9% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Dec 05 05:41 UTC. Mars: Naked eye; magnitude 0.5; direct motion; 89.8% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Nov 30 17:24 UTC. Ceres: Telescope; magnitude 7.7; retrograde motion; 98.1% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Jupiter: Naked eye; magnitude -2.2; direct motion; 99.2% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Conjunction with Moon in ecliptic longitude Nov 30 08:34 UTC. Saturn: Naked eye; magnitude 0.6; retrograde motion; 99.8% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Uranus: Binoculars; magnitude 5.6; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Neptune: Telescope; magnitude 7.7; retrograde motion; 100.0% illuminated. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot. Pluto: Substantial telescope; magnitude 14.6; direct motion; 100.0% illuminated. Below the horizon at 21:00 local apparent solar time, 45°N. Monday 00:00 UTC snapshot.

**Binoculars:** No fixed-sky Calendar object is classified for binocular observing this week.

**Small telescope:** NGC 559: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M103: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Triangulum Galaxy: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; M74: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Little Dumbbell Nebula: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance; Collinder 20: consult its dedicated finder and observing story for equipment guidance

story_candidates.dek: Achernar is a star in Eri of catalogue visual magnitude 0.45; its declination determines which latitudes can observe it.
story_candidates.body:
The stored catalogue gives a visual magnitude of 0.45. This is a catalogue value, not a prediction of its brightness this week. Lower magnitudes mean brighter objects; sky brightness and altitude affect whether you can see the star.

Its catalogue position is approximately right ascension 1h 37m and declination -57.2°. These reference coordinates describe its sky location; they are not an observing time or a current altitude.

At the almanac’s default latitude of 45° N, this star does not rise above the geometric horizon. These are geometric calculations from declination, excluding refraction and local obstructions. Darkness and the time of culmination must still be checked for the observing date and your location.

How to find it: Establish the preserved Eri constellation figure from its labeled reference stars, then use the target’s plotted position rather than searching for an isolated star.

Sources: Star Almanack’s stored fixed-object and expanded Bayer catalogues; accepted constellation figures and guiding-star routes. Visibility limits are original geometric calculations from catalogue declination, not weekly predictions.
